etymology: Hebrew bārā’, “to create.” In the Old Testament, used exclusively of God’s creative activity; never used of human making. The grammatical subject of bārā’ in its biblical uses is always God.
biblical_def: Bārā’ is the great Hebrew creation-verb—the word with which the Bible opens (in the beginning God created (bārā’) the heaven and the earth, Gen 1:1) and the word that is used uniformly across the Old Testament for God’s creative activity. Two grammatical features mark the verb as theologically distinctive. First, its grammatical subject is always God: bārā’ is not used of human creative making (for which other verbs are used: ‘āsāh, to make; yātsar, to form, as a potter forms clay); it is reserved for the activity that only God performs. Second, it does not require pre-existing material: while the verb can in some contexts describe creative ordering of existing material (as ‘āsāh typically does), in its supreme uses (Gen 1:1; Isa 40:26; Isa 45:7, 12, 18) it carries the sense of creation out of nothing—the bringing into being of what previously had no existence. The doctrine of creatio ex nihilo (creation out of nothing) is therefore grounded in the biblical use of bārā’. The verb appears at several theologically weighty hinges across the Old Testament. The creation of the heavens and the earth: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Gen 1:1). The creation of man in the image of God: so God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Gen 1:27—three uses of bārā’ in one verse). The creation of new heavens and a new earth in eschatological promise: for, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth: and the former shall not be remembered, nor come into mind (Isa 65:17). The pastoral promise of a renewed inward life: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me (Ps 51:10—David asking God to perform the very work only God can perform, on his sin-broken inner life). The verb’s structural use therefore traces an arc: God created in the beginning, God created man in His image, God will create new heavens and earth at the end, and God creates a clean heart in the redeemed sinner now. The verb in each case names the activity that only God performs, that requires no pre-existing material in its supreme uses, and that grounds the entire biblical doctrine of God as Creator distinct from and sovereign over all His creatures.
webster_summary: (Hebrew term.) Bārā’: to create; the great OT creation-verb whose grammatical subject is always God; foundation of the doctrine of creatio ex nihilo and of the biblical distinction between Creator and creature.

corruption_summary: Bārā’-shaped doctrine of creation is corrupted, in the contemporary cultural landscape, by the naturalistic-evolutionary account that has displaced the biblical Creator with impersonal processes—and by the inverse error of the theistic-evolution synthesis that has retained the word create while emptying it of the direct-divine-causation the Hebrew verb carries.
corruption_paragraphs: Naturalistic-evolutionary accounts of cosmic and biological origins have, across the past century and a half, displaced the biblical Creator with impersonal processes—quantum fluctuations producing the cosmos from nothing-via-physical-laws (which are themselves not nothing), Darwinian natural selection producing biological complexity from simpler ancestors via unguided mutation and selection, the long sweep of cosmic history understood as the playing-out of physical processes without divine involvement. The biblical doctrine of bārā’ refuses this. Creation is the personal act of God—the heaven and the earth, the man in His image, the new heavens and new earth, the clean heart in the redeemed sinner—and the verb’s grammatical subject is always God. The recovery is not chiefly scientific (the church has variously engaged the scientific questions and ought to continue) but doctrinal: the affirmation that God created, that He alone is Creator, that the cosmos is His artifact and not an unguided process, that He continues to create (the new heart, the new heavens and earth) in His sovereign activity across history and into eternity.

The opposite corruption is the theistic-evolution synthesis that has retained the word create while emptying it of the direct-divine-causation the Hebrew verb carries. On this account, God created by means of the evolutionary process; He set the process in motion at the beginning and superintended it providentially; the biblical creation accounts are taken as theological poetry compatible with the scientific narrative of long evolutionary development. The Christian tradition has variously assessed this synthesis, and the question of how God created remains contested across faithful Christians. But the integrity of the doctrine of creation requires preserving what bārā’ grammatically carries: the direct activity of God, the personal causation, the bringing into being of what would not otherwise exist—not merely the providential superintendence of impersonal processes. Recover both ends. Refuse the naturalistic displacement of the Creator, and preserve in any theistic-evolutionary synthesis the substantive direct-divine-causation the biblical verb carries. The God who created the heavens and the earth, who created man in His image, who will create new heavens and earth, and who creates a clean heart in the redeemed sinner is the personal Creator the biblical verb names—and any account of origins, ours or scientific, must preserve the substance of the verb if it would not lose the doctrine.

etymology: Hebrew yārē’, “to fear, reverence, be in awe of.” The verb covers a range from terror (of an enemy or judgment) to reverent awe (of God, parents, holy things). The noun yir’ah is “fear, reverence”—the central component of the fear of the LORD.
biblical_def: Yārē’ is the great Old Testament verb for fear, covering a semantic range from terror of an enemy or of judgment to the reverent awe of God Himself—and its supreme biblical use is in the phrase the fear of the LORD (yir’at YHWH), which the wisdom literature names as the beginning of wisdom, knowledge, and life. Proverbs 1:7: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction. Proverbs 9:10: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding. Proverbs 14:27: the fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, to depart from the snares of death. Proverbs 22:4: by humility and the fear of the LORD are riches, and honour, and life. Job 28:28: and unto man he said, Behold, the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom; and to depart from evil is understanding. Psalm 111:10: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: a good understanding have all they that do his commandments. The fear of the LORD is therefore structurally foundational to biblical wisdom. It is the beginning—the entry-point; what precedes any genuine wisdom, knowledge, or understanding. It is the fountain of life—the source from which true life flows. It is the disposition of soul that takes God seriously, that treats His commandments as binding, that walks before Him with the reverence proper to a creature standing before its holy Maker. The biblical fear of the LORD is not the cringing terror of the slave before the tyrant (that is the fear sin produces in the soul that knows itself unforgiven), but the awed reverence of the son before the Father whose love and holiness together call forth the response. The two combine: God’s holiness produces awe; God’s love makes the awe filial; the saint in whom both operate fears the LORD with the reverence Scripture commends and the love Scripture commands. Christ Himself was a man of the fear of the LORD: Isaiah 11:2 prophesies that the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon Him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and might, of knowledge and of the fear of the LORD; and Isaiah 11:3, and shall make him of quick understanding in the fear of the LORD. The Lord Jesus, perfect Man, lived in the perfect fear of the LORD—the awed reverent love of the Father whose will He came to do. The saint’s sanctification is, in part, the recovery of this disposition: the fear of the LORD restored to its proper place as the beginning of wisdom and the fountain of life.

corruption_summary: Yārē’-shaped fear of the LORD is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the systematic flattening of fear into respect—a translation move that empties the awe-component that Scripture insists upon—and by the inverse corruption that mistakes biblical fear of the LORD for the cringing terror of the slave, which is precisely what regenerate sons of the Father do not experience.
corruption_paragraphs: The systematic flattening of fear into respect is the most pervasive contemporary corruption. Modern translations and sermons regularly render fear of the LORD as reverence for the LORD or respect for the LORD, on the reasonable ground that fear in modern English has acquired primarily a terror-of-harm sense that does not capture the biblical category. The trade is real but costly. The biblical yir’at YHWH includes reverence and respect but is not exhausted by them; it carries an awe-component that recognizes the holiness, the majesty, the judgment-capacity, the unmediated weight of the holy God Himself. The believer who has been taught only respect for the LORD has not encountered the doctrine Proverbs names as the beginning of wisdom. The recovery is the substantial doctrine of God in His holiness: where God is preached and worshipped in His holiness, the fear of the LORD returns of itself, including its awe-component, including the proper trembling Scripture commends (him that trembleth at my word, Isa 66:2), without slipping into the cringing terror of the unforgiven.

The opposite corruption is the mistaking of biblical fear of the LORD for the cringing terror of the slave. The believer is taught that God is love and that perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18), and concludes that any fear of God in the regenerate is sub-Christian, a residue of legalism, a failure to grasp the gospel. The text Scripture actually gives is more nuanced. 1 John 4:18 contrasts perfect love with the fear that hath torment—the cringing terror of the soul that expects punishment—and announces that perfect love casts that fear out. It does not abolish the fear of the LORD that Scripture elsewhere commends as the beginning of wisdom; it abolishes the slavish terror of the unforgiven and replaces it with the filial reverence of the adopted son. The Father is to be feared with the awed love of the regenerate; the tyrant is to be feared with the cringing terror of the slave. The biblical pattern is the first, not the second; the contemporary church often loses both, leaving the believer with neither the proper awe nor the proper assurance. Recover both. Refuse the flattening that empties the fear of the LORD of its awe-component, and refuse the cringing slavish terror that the gospel has freed the saint from. The biblical fear of the LORD is the awed reverent love of the Father, the beginning of wisdom, the fountain of life—and the church saturated with it is the church whose worship has the seriousness, and whose discipleship has the substance, that the loss of the fear of the LORD has, in much of the contemporary church, quietly drained.

etymology: Greek martus (also spelled martur), “witness”; cognate verb martureō, “to bear witness.” The English word martyr derives from this Greek noun, the title eventually applied specifically to those whose witness was sealed with their blood.
biblical_def: Martus is the New Testament’s word for witness, and the etymology is structurally significant: the same noun that names the apostolic witness to the resurrection of Christ becomes, in early Christian usage, the title of those whose witness was sealed with their blood—the martyrs. The Greek word in the NT carries primarily the legal-and-courtroom sense: a witness is one who testifies under solemn responsibility to what he has seen, heard, and received. Christ Himself names the apostles witnesses in His commissioning: but ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth (Acts 1:8). Peter sets the apostolic vocation explicitly: him being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain: Whom God hath raised up, having loosed the pains of death... This Jesus hath God raised up, whereof we all are witnesses (Acts 2:23-32). Paul before Agrippa: but rise, and stand upon thy feet: for I have appeared unto thee for this purpose, to make thee a minister and a witness both of these things which thou hast seen, and of those things in the which I will appear unto thee (Acts 26:16). The apostolic martyria (witness) is therefore the historical witness to the resurrection of Christ—the founding deposit of Christian truth, codified in the New Testament Scriptures and proclaimed in the church’s mission. Christ Himself is named the supreme witness: and from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth (Rev 1:5); these things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God (Rev 3:14). The pattern of witness sealed with blood is set early. Stephen, called your martyr Stephen in the KJV translation of Acts 22:20 (the Greek is tou marturos sou Stephanou, “your witness Stephen”), demonstrates the costliness of apostolic witness in his being stoned to death for it. Antipas in Revelation 2:13 is called Christ’s faithful martyr (the Greek ho martus mou ho pistos) who was slain at Pergamos. By the second and third centuries the word had specifically denoted those whose witness was sealed with their blood—and the English martyr preserves that derivative sense. The biblical pattern of martus therefore has three dimensions. The apostolic witness to the resurrection is the founding deposit. The ongoing witness of the church (every saint a witness to what he knows of Christ, though not at the apostolic level of foundational deposit) is its continuation. And the witness-sealed-with-blood of the martyrs across every generation is the costliest form the same vocation has taken, in which the saint’s body itself becomes the seal of the truth he confessed.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Martus: witness; the NT word for those who testify to what they have seen, heard, and received; supremely the apostolic witness to the resurrection of Christ, and by extension the witness of every saint, sealed in the costliest form by the blood of the martyrs.

corruption_summary: Martus-shaped Christian witness is corrupted by the contemporary muting of explicit confession under cultural pressure (the believer trained to be Christian privately but not publicly)—and by the inverse loss of the costly-witness pattern in much of the comfortable Western church, where the cost of Stephen, of Antipas, of the apostles, and of the persecuted brethren of every age stands as a standing rebuke to the easy Christianity that has forgotten the price the early marturoi paid.
corruption_paragraphs: Cultural pressure has produced a generation of believers trained to be Christian privately but not publicly—to confess to God in prayer, to gather with the saints on Sunday, even to teach the children in the home, but to mute the explicit public witness that Acts 1:8 commands. The believer’s social, professional, and even ecclesial life is conducted with the Christian witness deliberately edited out: at work, the gospel is not named; with neighbors, the cross is not mentioned; in public conversation, the apostolic martyria is absent. The recovery is the recovery of the explicit witness Christ commissioned. Every believer is a witness; the apostolic deposit is to be proclaimed; the lordship of Christ is to be confessed in every sphere providence has placed the saint; the cost of the confession is to be accepted as the cost the early marturoi accepted. The contemporary church’s widespread silence is not Christian discretion; it is the muting of the very vocation Christ named at His ascension.

The opposite corruption is the loss of the costly-witness pattern in much of the comfortable Western church, where the cost of Stephen, of Antipas, of the apostles, and of the persecuted brethren of every age stands as a standing rebuke. The persecuted church across the centuries and across the present world—Christians in North Korea, in much of the Islamic world, in parts of the Hindu-nationalist East—continues to pay the price the early marturoi paid, with imprisonment, exile, family loss, torture, and death the regular cost of explicit confession of Christ. The comfortable Western church often does not even register the contrast between its own circumstances and the persecuted brethren’s, much less train its members for the possibility that the same cost may come closer in our own generation than the late-comfort era has imagined. The recovery is the recovery of the costly-witness vocation as the church’s standing pattern, with the cost varying historically (some generations pay it in blood, others in social marginalization, others in vocational loss) but the willingness to pay it being a non-negotiable mark of the saint who is in fact a martus of the resurrected Christ. So great a cloud of witnesses—Hebrews names the cloud, and the saints of the present age are to take their place among them.

etymology: Greek aiōnios, “eternal, age-long, of-the-age,” from aiōn (age, eon). The adjective carries both qualitative (pertaining to the eschatological age) and quantitative (everlasting, unending) senses, depending on context.
biblical_def: Aiōnios is the New Testament’s great adjective for eternal, and it carries some of the heaviest doctrinal freight in the Bible. The word is built from aiōn (age, eon), and its semantic range covers both the qualitative sense (pertaining to the coming age, the age-to-come, the eschatological age) and the quantitative sense (everlasting, unending in duration). Both senses are biblically operative, and the contexts make clear which is foreground in each use. Aiōnios qualifies several of the New Testament’s most weighted nouns. Eternal life (zōē aiōnios): the great gospel-promise word, used over forty times in the NT, especially in John’s Gospel and Epistles; John 3:16 (that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life); John 10:28 (and I give unto them eternal life); 1 John 5:11 (God hath given to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son). Eternal punishment (kolasis aiōnios): Matt 25:46 (and these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal)—the same adjective applied to both punishment and life in the same verse, making it grammatically untenable to read aiōnios as everlasting for the life and temporary for the punishment. Eternal fire (pur aiōnios): Matt 18:8; 25:41; Jude 7. Eternal destruction (olethros aiōnios): 2 Thess 1:9. Eternal God: Rom 16:26 (the eternal God); Heb 9:14 (the eternal Spirit). Eternal gospel: Rev 14:6. Eternal weight of glory: 2 Cor 4:17. Eternal covenant: Heb 13:20. Eternal kingdom: 2 Pet 1:11. Eternal inheritance: Heb 9:15. The grammar of aiōnios is therefore structurally important for several theological doctrines. The eternality of God (the eternal God; the eternal Spirit) is non-negotiable. The eternality of the gospel-given salvation is the believer’s great hope. The eternality of the punishment of the impenitent is the sober counterpart, against universalist readings that would make aiōnios kolasis a temporary corrective rather than an everlasting condition (the same word applied to life cannot mean different durations in the same Matthew 25:46). The category of the age to come, marked by aiōnios, is the structural eschatological category: the present age (this aiōn) is passing; the age to come is everlasting; the saints belong to the age to come and live in this age as those whose home and inheritance are in the next.

corruption_summary: Aiōnios is corrupted, on one side, by the universalist readings that would make aiōnios kolasis (eternal punishment) mean age-long corrective against the grammatical parallel with aiōnios zōē (eternal life) in the same Matt 25:46—and on the other by the present-age-only register that has lost the eschatological weight of the age to come as the structural orientation of Christian life.
corruption_paragraphs: The universalist corruption of aiōnios attempts to read eternal punishment in Matt 25:46 as merely age-long corrective—a temporary purifying discipline from which the recipient eventually emerges purified. The grammatical move is untenable: the same adjective in the same verse qualifies both punishment and life; if aiōnios in life eternal means everlasting (as universalists typically concede, since they want the saints to have everlasting life), then aiōnios in everlasting punishment must mean everlasting too—and the universalist reading collapses on its own grammar. The same adjective cannot mean two different durations in the same verse depending on which noun the interpreter prefers. The orthodox tradition has therefore consistently read aiōnios kolasis as everlasting punishment—a sober doctrine, not lightly preached, but biblically grounded and structurally bound to the eternality of the corresponding life it stands against. The recovery of the doctrine is the recovery of the gospel’s seriousness: the offer is real, the warning is real, and both run the same eternal duration the same Greek adjective names.

The opposite corruption is the present-age-only register that has lost the eschatological weight of the age to come as the structural orientation of Christian life. The category aiōnios in many of its NT uses carries the qualitative sense (pertaining to the age-to-come, the eschatological age) alongside the quantitative sense (everlasting); both belong to its meaning. Contemporary preaching often loses both. The believer is not regularly oriented toward the age to come as the home and inheritance to which the present age is the antechamber; the eschatological future is bracketed; the Christian life becomes a present-age project of personal flourishing rather than a pilgrimage toward the consummating age. Recover the doctrine, and the saint recovers his proper orientation: this present age is passing, the age to come is everlasting, the saint belongs to the age to come and lives in this age as a sojourner whose home is elsewhere. The eternal weight of glory of 2 Cor 4:17, the eternal inheritance of Heb 9:15, the eternal kingdom of 2 Pet 1:11—these are not vague hopes for after-death continuity but the substantive realities of the age to come that aiōnios names with both qualitative and quantitative weight.

etymology: Greek hagiasmos, “sanctification, holiness,” from hagiazō (to make holy, sanctify), from hagios (holy). Both the act of sanctification and the resulting state of holiness.
biblical_def: Hagiasmos is the New Testament’s precise word for sanctification—both the act by which God sets His people apart and progressively conforms them to His holiness, and the resulting state of holiness in the redeemed. The word stands at the heart of one of the great structural doctrines of Reformed theology: the distinction-and-relation between justification (the legal declaration of righteousness through faith in Christ) and sanctification (the moral transformation of the believer by the Spirit). Both are works of God; both are received by faith; both are anchored in union with Christ; neither can be collapsed into the other; neither can be separated from the other. Paul ties them together in 1 Corinthians 6:11: and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God. Sanctification has both a definitive moment (the believer is set apart at conversion, called saints [hagioi, holy ones] across the NT from that moment onward) and a progressive course (the believer is being progressively conformed to the image of Christ across his Christian life). 1 Thessalonians 4:3 sets the will of God explicitly: for this is the will of God, even your sanctification. Hebrews 12:14: follow peace with all men, and holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord. 2 Corinthians 7:1: let us cleanse ourselves from all filthiness of the flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God. The means of sanctification are several. The Word: sanctify them through thy truth: thy word is truth (John 17:17). The Spirit: through sanctification of the Spirit (2 Thess 2:13; 1 Pet 1:2). Providential dealing: whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth (Heb 12:6). The means of grace (Word, sacraments, prayer, gathering). The saint’s active cooperation: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure (Phil 2:12-13)—divine working and human working, each in its proper relation. The eschatological end of sanctification is the perfect conformity to Christ at His appearing: we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2). Sanctification is therefore the long arc of the believer’s being made holy as the Holy One who has set him apart is holy—a work begun at conversion, sustained across the Christian life, and consummated at the resurrection in the perfect likeness of Christ.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Hagiasmos: sanctification, holiness; both the act of being set apart unto God and the progressive moral transformation of the believer toward the image of Christ; structural doctrine of Reformed theology, distinguished from justification but inseparable from it.
webster_full: SANCTIFICATION, n. — 1. The act of God’s grace by which the affections of men are purified or alienated from sin and the world, and exalted to a supreme love to God. 2. The act of consecrating or of setting apart for a sacred purpose. 3. The state of being sanctified; the state of being holy and devoted to God.

corruption_summary: Hagiasmos-shaped sanctification is corrupted, on one side, by the antinomian-grace tradition that has separated sanctification from the gospel and treated it as an optional addition to a justification-only salvation—and on the other by the perfectionist traditions that have collapsed sanctification’s long progressive course into a single decisive crisis-experience producing complete sinlessness in this life.
corruption_paragraphs: The antinomian-grace tradition has separated sanctification from the gospel and treated it as an optional addition to a justification-only salvation. On this account, the believer is justified by faith in Christ, declared righteous, and need not concern himself unduly with the progressive moral transformation toward holiness that the New Testament uniformly assumes will follow. The result is a gospel-claim without any gospel-life: claims of conversion paired with patterns of life that show no progressive sanctification, doctrinal precision divorced from any visible holiness, profession without the corresponding moral transformation the Spirit produces in every regenerate saint. Scripture refuses the separation. Justification and sanctification are distinct gifts but never separable; the Christ who justifies also sanctifies; the Spirit who applies the imputed righteousness of Christ to the believer also indwells him and progressively conforms him to Christ’s image. The recovery is the integrated doctrine: salvation is a Christ-given complex of justification, sanctification, and glorification, in which the believer is declared righteous, progressively made holy, and at last fully conformed to Christ—all gifts of grace, all received by faith, all in their proper distinction-and-relation.

The opposite corruption is the perfectionist tradition that has collapsed sanctification’s long progressive course into a single decisive crisis-experience producing complete sinlessness in this life. Various Wesleyan, Holiness, and Keswick traditions have taught versions of this: a second blessing, an entire sanctification, a complete consecration that eradicates indwelling sin and produces sinless Christian perfection in the present. Scripture refuses this also. 1 John 1:8: if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; the saint sins, confesses, is forgiven, is being progressively sanctified, and will be fully conformed only at the resurrection. Sanctification is progressive across the Christian life, with seasons of more visible progress and seasons of struggle, but does not reach perfection in this present age. Recover both ends. Refuse the antinomian separation of sanctification from the gospel, and refuse the perfectionist collapse of progressive sanctification into a single crisis-experience. The biblical pattern is the long, Spirit-wrought, progressive conformity of the saint to the image of Christ—begun at conversion, sustained across the Christian life through the appointed means of grace, and consummated only at the resurrection in the perfect likeness of the Lord.

Antinomianism separates sanctification from the gospel; perfectionism collapses its long course into a crisis-experience; biblical hagiasmos is the long Spirit-wrought progressive conformity of the saint to Christ, consummated only at the resurrection.

etymology: Greek apokalupsis, “an uncovering, revelation, disclosure,” from apokaluptō (to uncover, reveal), from apo- (off, from) + kaluptō (to cover, veil). The literal sense is off-veiling: the removing of a covering so that what was previously hidden is now seen.
biblical_def: Apokalupsis is the New Testament’s great word for revelation—the divine uncovering of what would otherwise remain hidden. The word governs three major theological categories. First, the revelation of God in general: His self-disclosure in creation, in providence, in the prophetic word, and supremely in His Son. Romans 1:18 names the present revelation of God’s wrath against unrighteousness: for the wrath of God is revealed (apokaluptetai) from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men. Romans 16:25-26 names the revelation of the mystery of the gospel, kept secret since the world began but now made manifest: according to the revelation of the mystery, which was kept secret since the world began, But now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith. Second, the revelation of God to specific recipients for the founding-and-shaping of the apostolic gospel. Paul received his gospel by the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal 1:12); he writes of visions and revelations of the Lord (2 Cor 12:1); the apostles and prophets received the foundational revelations on which the church is built (Eph 2:20; 3:5). Third, and supremely climactic, the eschatological revelation: the parousia or apokalupsis of Christ at His second coming, the great unveiling at the end of the age. 1 Corinthians 1:7: waiting for the coming (apokalupsis) of our Lord Jesus Christ. 2 Thessalonians 1:7: when the Lord Jesus shall be revealed (apokalupsei) from heaven with his mighty angels. 1 Peter 1:7: that the trial of your faith... might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing (apokalupsei) of Jesus Christ. 1 Peter 1:13: hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation (apokalupsei) of Jesus Christ. The last book of the NT itself is named after this word: The Revelation (Apokalupsis) of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass (Rev 1:1). The book of Revelation is the climactic apokalupsis: the divine uncovering of what God will do at the end of the age, given to John on Patmos and through him to the churches of every age. The biblical doctrine of revelation is therefore structurally Trinitarian and Christological: God reveals; the Father gives the revelation to the Son; the Son gives it to His servants by His Spirit through His apostles and prophets; the church receives it in Scripture; the final and consummating revelation is the unveiling of Christ Himself at His coming, when every eye shall see Him and the saints shall be like Him.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) corruption_summary: Apokalupsis-shaped doctrine of revelation is corrupted, on one side, by the continuing-revelation traditions (charismatic, Roman Catholic, Mormon) that have placed extra-canonical sources on a level with the apostolic revelation closed in the New Testament—and on the other by the cessationist over-correction that has so feared continuing-revelation excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age work of illumination and applied revelation through the closed canon.
corruption_paragraphs: The continuing-revelation corruption takes several forms across various traditions. Roman Catholicism has historically placed church tradition on a level with Scripture as the source of divine revelation. Mormonism has added the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price as continuing revelations. Charismatic and Pentecostal movements often function with prophecies and personal revelations that, while formally distinguished from Scripture, in practice exercise authority comparable to it. The Protestant doctrine of sola Scriptura insists that the foundational and authoritative revelation of God for the post-apostolic church is the closed canon of Scripture; the apostolic revelation, with the apostles having no successors in their unique founding office, is complete; subsequent claims of revelation are to be tested against Scripture and never to be placed on a level with it. The recovery is the recovery of the closed canon as the rule of faith and life, the sole infallible standard, the foundation upon which the church is built.

The opposite corruption is the cessationist over-correction that has so feared continuing-revelation excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age work of illumination and applied revelation through the closed canon. The doctrine that the foundational revelation is closed (the canon is complete; no new Scripture-level revelations are being given; the apostles have no successors in their unique office) does not require the conclusion that the Spirit no longer illumines, applies, guides, convicts, or speaks through the closed canon to particular saints in particular providences. The historic Reformed tradition has consistently distinguished between foundational revelation (closed) and the Spirit’s ongoing application of the foundational revelation to His people in their particular situations (continuing). The Westminster Confession (1.6): the whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture: unto which nothing at any time is to be added, whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men. Nevertheless, we acknowledge the inward illumination of the Spirit of God to be necessary for the saving understanding of such things as are revealed in the Word. Both ends are required: closed canon as the foundational revelation, and ongoing Spirit-mediated illumination and application as the present-age work the same Spirit performs through the Word He inspired. Recover both, and the doctrine of revelation stands biblically and pastorally where it should: foundational and complete, but presently applied by the Spirit who is no less active for the canon’s closure.

etymology: Greek diakonia, “service, ministry, attendance,” from diakonos (servant, attendant; the source of English deacon); possibly from dia- (through) + a root meaning to hasten, the literal sense being running-through in service.
biblical_def: Diakonia is the New Testament’s great word for service or ministry—a category that runs across both the most ordinary helping-service in the body of Christ and the most exalted gospel-ministry of the apostles. The Greek word can name the ministry of waiting tables (Acts 6:1, their widows were neglected in the daily ministration (diakonia)), the ministry of the diaconal office (Acts 6:4, where the apostles set apart men for this work that they themselves might give attention to prayer and the ministry of the word), the ministry of giving (2 Cor 8:4, the Macedonian saints’ fellowship of the ministering (diakonia) to the saints), the ministry of the apostolic office (Acts 1:17, 25; 20:24; 21:19; Rom 11:13), the ministry of the new covenant (2 Cor 3:6-9), the ministry of reconciliation (2 Cor 5:18), and the ministry of the Spirit (2 Cor 3:8). The breadth is structural and important. Diakonia in the NT vocabulary covers everything from the most humble physical service to the most exalted gospel-ministry, holding them under one word and thereby insisting that all true Christian work is service. Even Christ Himself is named in this register: even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister (diakonēsai), and to give his life a ransom for many (Matt 20:28—the verb behind minister is the cognate). Two structural points follow. First, the gifts of the Spirit are distributed for diakonia: now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of administrations (diakoniōn, plural of diakonia), but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal (1 Cor 12:4-7); Eph 4:11-12, and he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; For the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry (diakonia), for the edifying of the body of Christ. The whole body, by its diverse Spirit-given gifts, exercises diakonia; every saint has a ministry; the church functions when every member is engaged in the service the Spirit has equipped him to render. Second, the diaconal office (servants set apart for particular service in the church, especially to the physical needs of the saints) is one specific application of the broader category. 1 Tim 3:8-13 lays out the qualifications for diakonoi as one of the two NT offices alongside episkopoi (elders/overseers). The deacons are honored, qualified men set apart for service in the church, freeing the elders for the ministry of the Word and prayer (Acts 6) and themselves rendering substantial spiritual ministry through their physical service. The recovery of biblical diakonia is therefore the recovery of the whole-body model of ministry: every saint a servant, every gift given for ministry, the diaconal office held in honor as a real spiritual ministry, and the apostolic-and-pastoral ministry of the Word as the chief but not the only service in the body.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Diakonia: service, ministry, attendance; the NT’s broad word covering everything from the humblest helping-service to the most exalted apostolic gospel-ministry, with the diaconal office as one specific application alongside the wider Spirit-gifted ministry of every saint.

corruption_summary: Diakonia-shaped ministry is corrupted, on one side, by the professional-clergy model that has collapsed all biblical ministry into the work of a paid ministerial class and disabled the whole-body ministry the NT assumes—and on the other by the over-democratization that has erased the proper distinctions between the apostolic-pastoral ministry of the Word and the diaconal-and-general ministry of all saints, against the New Testament’s explicit ordering.
corruption_paragraphs: The professional-clergy model has, across the post-Reformation centuries and especially in modern Protestant practice, often collapsed all biblical ministry into the work of a paid ministerial class. The pastor is the minister; the laity attend; the saints come on Sunday to receive the ministry of the professional and return to their secular lives without exercising the Spirit-gifted ministry the NT assumes of every member of the body. The result is a passive congregation, an exhausted pastorate (carrying alone what the whole body was given to share), and the loss of the rich New Testament category of diakonia as the active ministry of every saint in the body. The recovery is the recovery of whole-body ministry. Every saint has a gift; every gift is given for diakonia; the perfecting of the saints is for the work of the ministry (Eph 4:12); the pastor’s special work is the equipping of the saints to do the ministry, not the doing of all the ministry himself. The church saturated with this whole-body diakonia is the church the apostles built and the church for which the present passive-clergy-active model is a poor substitute.

The opposite corruption is the over-democratization that has erased the proper distinctions between the apostolic-pastoral ministry of the Word and the diaconal-and-general ministry of all saints. On this account, everyone is equally a minister in every sense; the distinction between elders/overseers (charged with the ministry of the Word, doctrine, discipline) and the wider body (gifted for various ministries of service) is muted; the special qualifications for the office of elder and deacon (1 Tim 3; Tit 1) are treated as optional; the church becomes an undifferentiated body in which no one is particularly responsible for the ministry of the Word and no one is particularly accountable for it. Scripture insists upon both: the wide ministry of every saint (so the whole body is engaged) and the particular ministry of qualified officers (so the Word is faithfully preached, the sacraments rightly administered, the discipline appropriately exercised, the flock rightly shepherded). Recover both. Refuse the professional-clergy collapse that disables the body, and refuse the over-democratization that erases the proper offices. The biblical pattern is whole-body diakonia with ordered officers within it—every saint a minister and qualified men set apart for the particular ministries the NT specifies.

etymology: Greek presbuteros, “elder,” literally older one, comparative of presbus (old man). The same Greek root produces English presbyter and priest (the latter via the medieval contraction of presbyter). In NT usage, the title of the chief ordained office of the local church, used interchangeably with episkopos (bishop, overseer).
biblical_def: Presbuteros is the New Testament’s great word for the office of elder—one of two ecclesial offices recognized in the apostolic church (alongside diakonos, deacon). The word literally means older one, the comparative of presbus (old man); but in NT ecclesial usage it has become a technical term for the office, regardless of the literal age of the office-holder (though Paul does specifically charge Timothy, let no man despise thy youth, 1 Tim 4:12, indicating the office-holders were typically though not invariably older men). Several structural features mark the biblical office. First, plurality: the NT pattern is uniformly multiple elders in each local church. Paul and Barnabas ordained them elders in every church (Acts 14:23); Paul calls for the elders of the church at Ephesus (Acts 20:17, the plural); Titus is to ordain elders in every city (Tit 1:5, the plural); James says let him call for the elders of the church (James 5:14, the plural). The single-pastor model that has become widespread in modern Protestantism is not the NT pattern; the NT pattern is a plurality of elders shepherding each local congregation together. Second, interchangeability with episkopos: the two words name the same office. Paul calls the same men in Acts 20 first elders (presbuteroi, v. 17) and then overseers (episkopoi, v. 28); Titus 1:5-7 describes the same men first as elders (v. 5) and then as bishops (v. 7, episkopos). The later development of bishop as a distinct higher office over multiple presbyters is post-apostolic; the NT knows one office named by two interchangeable titles. Third, qualifications: 1 Timothy 3:1-7 and Titus 1:6-9 list the qualifications, which are weighted toward character (blameless, husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, patient, not a brawler, not covetous, ruling his own house well) and explicitly include the ability to teach sound doctrine and refute gainsayers. Fourth, function: elders rule (1 Tim 5:17), shepherd the flock (1 Pet 5:1-4), watch for souls (Heb 13:17), exhort and convince by sound doctrine (Tit 1:9), feed the flock (Acts 20:28), and exercise spiritual oversight on Christ’s behalf. Some elders particularly labor in word and doctrine (1 Tim 5:17), suggesting a distinction within the eldership between those gifted especially for the teaching ministry and those who, while qualified to teach, exercise their primary ministry in the ruling-and-shepherding function. The recovery of biblical eldership is therefore the recovery of plural, character-qualified, congregationally-shepherding ministry, distinguished from the various ecclesial corruptions: hierarchical bishop-priest-deacon ranking that exalts one elder over others; single-pastor model that leaves one man bearing what the NT assigns to a plurality; democratized congregationalism that erases the office entirely; lax qualification practices that ordain men whose character does not meet the apostolic standard.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Presbuteros: elder; the chief ordained office of the local NT church, used interchangeably with episkopos (bishop, overseer); plural in each congregation; qualified by character; exercising rule, shepherding, teaching, and spiritual oversight under Christ.

corruption_summary: Presbuteros-shaped eldership is corrupted, in the present church landscape, by the single-pastor model (one man bearing what NT plurality assigns to multiple), the hierarchical episcopal model (raising bishop as a higher office over multiple presbyters, post-apostolically), the lax-qualification practices (ordaining men whose character does not meet the apostolic standard), and the democratized congregationalism that erases the office entirely.
corruption_paragraphs: The single-pastor model is the most pervasive contemporary corruption among Protestant churches that retain the office of elder at all. The NT pattern is multiple elders in each local congregation, sharing the rule, the shepherding, the teaching, and the oversight; the post-Reformation Protestant pattern has often collapsed this into the single senior pastor (with assistants, perhaps, but not co-equal elders) carrying the bulk of the ministry alone. The result is exhausted pastors, dependent congregations, and the loss of the mutual accountability the NT plural-eldership pattern preserves. The recovery is the recovery of plural eldership: multiple character-qualified men, ordained to share the ministry of the Word, the shepherding of the flock, and the spiritual oversight of the congregation. The hierarchical episcopal model that distinguishes bishop as a higher office over multiple presbyters is a post-apostolic development (clear by Ignatius of Antioch, ca. 110, but not in the NT itself); the recovery of biblical eldership preserves the equality of elders within the plurality, with such functional distinctions (teaching elder vs. ruling elder, as in some Reformed polities) as the NT itself indicates.

The lax-qualification corruption is the broader and more pastorally damaging contemporary one. The qualifications of 1 Tim 3 and Tit 1 are weighted toward character—blameless, husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach, not given to wine, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, patient, not a brawler, not covetous, ruling his own house well, having his children in subjection, not a novice, having a good report of them which are without. Many contemporary ordinations proceed without serious examination of these qualifications; men are ordained whose lives bear credible moral charges, whose families are disordered, whose teaching is at best superficial, whose qualification for the office is functionally limited to a personable temperament and an inclination toward ministry. The recovery is the recovery of the qualifications as a real test, with examining elders and congregations refusing to ordain those who do not meet the apostolic standard, however gifted in other respects. The democratized-congregationalism corruption at the other extreme erases the office entirely, treating the congregation as functionally undifferentiated and recognizing no particular office of elder over it. Both extremes miss the NT pattern: plural, character-qualified, congregationally-shepherding eldership under Christ, with the deacons supplying the diaconal service alongside, and the whole body engaged in the ministry the Spirit has given to every member.

etymology: Greek charisma, “a gift of grace, free gift,” from charis (grace, favor); plural charismata. The word designates both saving gifts (eternal life, Rom 6:23) and the diverse gifts of the Spirit distributed to members of the body.
biblical_def: Charisma is the New Testament’s precise word for a gift of grace—the Spirit-given endowment freely bestowed on the church and on individual saints for the building up of the body and the accomplishing of God’s purposes. The cognate noun charis (grace, free favor) makes the etymology theologically pointed: every charisma is a graced gift, freely given, not earned, distributed by the Spirit’s sovereign apportioning rather than the recipient’s merit. The word covers a broad semantic range across the NT. At its highest, charisma names the gift of salvation itself: for the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God (to charisma tou theou) is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom 6:23). Eternal life is the supreme charisma: grace-given, not earned, freely bestowed on those who believe in Christ. The word covers the spiritual gifts distributed to members of the body for the upbuilding of the church. Romans 12:6-8: having then gifts (charismata) differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness. 1 Corinthians 12:4-11 lists nine gifts: word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith, gifts of healing, working of miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, divers kinds of tongues, interpretation of tongues. 1 Corinthians 12:28-30 lists various offices and gifts: apostles, prophets, teachers, miracles, gifts of healing, helps, governments, diversities of tongues. Ephesians 4:11 lists the gifts of ascended Christ to the church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers. 1 Peter 4:10-11: as every man hath received the gift (charisma), even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth. Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, every believer has at least one charisma: as every man hath received the gift; the gifts are distributed across the body, not concentrated in a few. Second, the gifts are diverse: the body has many members, and the Spirit distributes the gifts variously according to His sovereign will (1 Cor 12:11, but all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will). Third, the gifts are given for the body: but the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal (1 Cor 12:7); they are not for private flourishing but for corporate building. Fourth, the gifts must be exercised in love: 1 Cor 13 sits between the two gift-chapters precisely to insist that without love the gifts are nothing and profit nothing. Fifth, the gifts are to be cultivated and stirred up: Paul charges Timothy to stir up the gift of God, which is in thee (2 Tim 1:6). The recovery of biblical charismata is therefore the recovery of the whole-body, diverse, love-grounded, actively-stewarded ministry of every Spirit-equipped saint in the building up of the church.

corruption_summary: Charisma-shaped gifting is corrupted, on one side, by the charismatic-movement excesses that have elevated certain showy gifts (tongues, miracles, prophetic words) above the broader range of NT gifts and treated them as the markers of true spirituality—and on the other by the cessationist over-correction that has so feared the excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age distribution of gifts to the body, against the NT pattern that every believer has a gift and the body functions when every gift is exercised.
corruption_paragraphs: The charismatic-movement excesses have, across the past century and especially in their Pentecostal and neo-Pentecostal forms, elevated certain showy gifts (tongues, miraculous healings, prophetic words, falling-in-the-Spirit phenomena) above the broader range of NT gifts and treated them as the markers of true spirituality. The result is a Christianity in which the believer who does not exhibit these particular gifts is implicitly second-class, the church gathering is shaped around the cultivation and display of these gifts, and the broader range of NT charismata (giving, helping, governing, mercy, teaching, exhortation) is muted as comparatively unspectacular. Scripture refuses the hierarchy. 1 Cor 12 explicitly insists that the body needs the diverse gifts; that the comparatively-less-visible gifts (helps, governments) are no less important than the comparatively-more-visible (tongues, miracles); and that no member of the body may say to another I have no need of thee. The recovery is the recovery of the whole NT gift-catalog: every saint gifted, every gift important, the showy and the unshowy alike given for the building up of the body.

The opposite corruption is the cessationist over-correction that has so feared the charismatic-movement excesses that it has muted the Spirit’s present-age distribution of gifts to the body. Some cessationist traditions have effectively dropped the categories of charismata from active church life: the saints are not catechized in the doctrine of gifts; gifts-discernment is not practiced; the body operates largely through the formal offices and the volunteerism of those who happen to step forward, with no systematic recognition that the Spirit has equipped every member with particular gifts for particular ministries. The recovery is the recovery of the doctrine without the excesses: every believer has a charisma, every gift is given for the body, the gifts are diverse and the body needs them all, the gifts are to be exercised in love and stewarded with diligence. The cessationist question of whether some particular gifts (tongues, miracles, prophecy in its foundational-revelatory form) have ceased with the apostolic age is a legitimate intramural Reformed discussion; but the broader pattern of Spirit-distributed charismata to every member of the body is not in question and must be recovered if the church is to function as the body Scripture describes.

etymology: Greek proskuneō, “to bow down, do obeisance, worship,” from pros- (toward) + kuneō (to kiss); the etymology suggests the gesture of kissing-toward (the hand or feet of) the one honored, as in the ancient practice of prostrate reverence before kings and deities.
biblical_def: Proskuneō is the New Testament’s great verb for worship—and the etymology is theologically pointed. The word is built from pros- (toward) + kuneō (to kiss), suggesting the literal gesture of bowing-and-kissing-toward, the prostrate physical reverence with which subjects of the ancient world honored kings and deities. The verb is therefore embodied, not merely mental or affective: proskuneō is the bowing-down before, the prostrating-oneself toward, the embodied act of homage that confesses with the body what the heart acknowledges—that the One worshipped is supremely worthy. The supreme biblical application is to God Himself. The First Commandment grounds it: Thou shalt have no other gods before me; the worship that the verb names is to be given to God alone. Christ’s answer to Satan’s third temptation makes the doctrine explicit: then saith Jesus unto him, Get thee hence, Satan: for it is written, Thou shalt worship (proskunēseis) the Lord thy God, and him only shalt thou serve (Matt 4:10, quoting Deut 6:13). The exclusivity of true worship is not a sectarian preference; it is the divinely-grounded standard, and Christ Himself sets it. The biblical doctrine therefore has its strict positive and its strict negative. Positive: worship is to be rendered to God, freely, fully, with the whole self including the body. The Samaritan woman’s encounter with Christ at the well draws out the further specification: but the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him. God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth (John 4:23-24). True worship is therefore embodied (involving the body, the bowing, the gesture, the voice) and yet also spiritual (engaging the inner spirit, not mere outward form) and according to truth (according to the truth God has revealed of Himself, not invented by the worshipper). Negative: worship is not to be rendered to creatures. Cornelius bowing to Peter is corrected: and as Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man (Acts 10:25-26). John bowing to the angel in Revelation is twice corrected: and I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant... worship God (Rev 19:10; 22:8-9). The exclusivity is firm: no apostle, no angel, no saint, no created being is to receive the worship that belongs to God alone. The supreme Christological inference is therefore unmistakable. Christ Himself receives worship: at His birth (Matt 2:11, the wise men); during His ministry (Matt 9:18 the ruler; Matt 14:33 the disciples after the storm; Matt 15:25 the Syro-Phoenician woman; Matt 28:9 the women after the resurrection); after His resurrection (Matt 28:17 the disciples); in heaven (Heb 1:6 the angels at the Father’s command; Rev 5:14 the elders and living creatures). And He does not refuse it. If worship God alone is the standard and Christ accepts proskuneō from human and angelic worshippers, then Christ is God: the inference the NT writers draw, and the inference that grounds the Trinitarian worship of the church across every century.
webster_summary: (Greek term.) Proskuneō: to worship, bow down, do obeisance; literally to kiss toward; the great NT verb for the embodied homage rendered to God alone (per the First Commandment and Christ’s Matt 4:10), refused by apostles and angels, received by Christ as evidence of His deity.

corruption_summary: Proskuneō-shaped worship is corrupted, on one side, by the disembodied register of much contemporary Western worship that has reduced the bodily homage of proskuneō to a primarily intellectual or affective inward act with little bodily expression—and on the other by the idolatrous direction of worship toward creatures (saints, angels, images, the Mary of Marian devotion, the man-centered worship of celebrity culture), against the First Commandment and Christ’s explicit Matt 4:10 standard.
corruption_paragraphs: The disembodied register of much contemporary Western worship has reduced proskuneō to a primarily intellectual or affective inward act with little bodily expression. The Greek verb is bodily: to bow down, to kiss toward, to prostrate. The biblical pattern is bodily: lifted hands (Ps 28:2; 63:4; 134:2; 1 Tim 2:8), bowed heads (Gen 24:26; Ex 34:8), bent knees (1 Kgs 8:54; Eph 3:14; Phil 2:10), prostrate bodies (Ezek 1:28; 3:23; 11:13; Matt 17:6; Rev 1:17). The disembodied contemporary register—hands in pockets, eyes on the screen, body still and uninvolved—has lost something the Greek verb physically names. The recovery is not the manufactured embodiment of stage-managed performance but the natural recovery of the body’s involvement in worship as the soul engages God: lifted hands when the heart is moved to lift, bowed head when the soul is moved to bow, kneeling when the moment calls for kneeling. The same verb the NT uses for the worship Christ accepts is the verb that has the body in it; the recovery is the recovery of the body’s involvement in the worship the Bible names.

The opposite corruption is the idolatrous direction of worship toward creatures, against the First Commandment and Christ’s Matt 4:10 standard. Various traditions have done this in various ways: Marian devotion that addresses to Mary the proskuneō Christ’s teaching reserved for God alone; the veneration of saints that escalates from honor into worship; the use of images that, however its defenders distinguish ‘veneration’ from ‘adoration,’ visually directs the worshipper’s posture toward the image rather than toward God; the celebrity-pastor culture of contemporary Western evangelicalism that, however unintentionally, trains the affections toward men rather than toward Christ; the entertainment-shaped worship that orients the gathering around what moves the worshipper rather than around the God who is worshipped. The biblical refusal is sharp and uniform: Peter refuses Cornelius’s proskuneō, the angel refuses John’s, Christ accepts proskuneō from all who offer it because He is God and the worship belongs to Him. The recovery is the strict First-Commandment-grounded exclusivity of true worship: to God alone, in spirit and in truth, with the body and the soul engaged, after the pattern the New Testament uniformly assumes and that Christ Himself sets at the climax of His wilderness temptations.
